newsitem.title: GERMANY: Polish thirst leads E.Europe coffee market growth.
newsitem.headline: Polish thirst leads E.Europe coffee market growth.

text.p: Poland has taken the lead in the fledgling coffee markets of eastern Europe as its citizens' purchasing power rises with economic growth, wholesalers and traders in western Europe said.
Coffee-drinking fits in easily with hospitality traditions among Poland's 40-million strong population and annual consumption has risen five-fold since 1989 to two kilos (4.4 lbs) each.
"There is quite fantastic potential in Poland," said a source at a large coffee trading company.
"Its annual green (unroasted) coffee consumption could easily reach 150,000 tonnes from around 90,000 at the moment."
Analysts put East Europe's per-capita average at below two kilos, but in the former USSR, it is just a few hundred grams.
By comparison, Germany's figure this year is 6.9 kilos.
"There is no law saying less coffee should be drunk in Warsaw than in Berlin," said Hasso Kaempfe, board member at Germany's Tchibo Frisch-Roest-Kaffee GmbH.
Traders said the whole region is back on track towards demand growth after falls in 1994 and 1995 when world coffee prices were high.
"Coffee sales in nearly all countries apart from Slovakia have risen and we base our plans for next year on five percent growth," said Kaempfe on Tchibo's operations in the region.
"That's less than we hoped for in the early 1990s, but it's important....to be present when sales do pick up dramatically."
German coffee expert F.O. Licht sees central and eastern European green bean consumption rising from 1996/97.
"Almost certainly within the first quarter of the new century, coffee will become a mass market drink, at least in the urban centres," Licht said of the region.
Traders said large international coffee roasters (wholesalers) were the clear winners in the expanding market.
"They are creating their own markets through aggressive branding and advertising," said a green coffee trader.

This is good for consumption but at the same time threatens local roasters, their western suppliers, and direct sales of green coffee, roasted and instant coffee from countries of origin, the trader added.
But only large firms have the means to handle political and tariff problems and survive lulls when purchasing power sags.
Apart from Germany's Tchibo, Dutch-American Douwe Egberts Sara Lee (DE), German-American Kraft Jacobs Suchard (KJS), and Swiss Nestle SA are all in the battle for market share.

Tchibo says it has a combined market share of 24 percent in Poland, the Czech republic, Slovakia and Hungary. It is the market leader in Poland and the Czech republic while leadership in Slovakia is held by a local firm and Hungary is dominated by DE, which claims 39 percent of all sales.
Western presence in the Hungarian and Czech markets is at least 80 percent, in Poland it is 60 percent but is just 20 percent in Slovakia.

While the four countries have a tradition drinking roasted ground coffee, tea-drinking nations in the former east bloc offer vast opportunities for sales of instant coffee, with its similar preparation method.

A Nestle spokesman spoke of "a large pent-up demand that is being satisfied." He did not give regional growth rates or forecasts, but traders said Nestle's Nescafe brand was important in Russia, Romania, Ukraine, Belarus and former Yugoslavia.

In raw materials trends, traders saw quality arabica coffees gaining share from cheaper robustas, especially competitively priced Brazilian coffees, as the region develops a taste for higher quality blends.
